facts.text: Prophet Lebioda's cult flourished about one hundred fifty years before the present day, during his own lifetime.
Prophet Lebioda was originally a simple shepherd who preached sermons and told parables about life, gods, and men.
Prophet Lebioda gathered a large group of followers who tried to live according to his teachings.
Prophet Lebioda died in old age after being set on fire and devoured by a dragon he was trying to exorcise.
The exorcism Prophet Lebioda attempted was meant to stop a dragon from preying on sheep belonging to Kaedweni villagers.
Prophet Lebioda's death was declared a martyrdom, and his recovered bones were placed in a sarcophagus in Novigrad.
On certain festivities, Prophet Lebioda's bones are taken from his sarcophagus so the pious can kiss them.
Though the original cult around Prophet Lebioda largely died out after his death, his teachings were preserved in a text called the Good Book, a collection of parables and anecdotes.
Worship of Prophet Lebioda's teachings has spread across nearly all of Redania, gradually displacing the older cult of Kreve.
The Order of the Flaming Rose is a militant arm associated with the spread of Lebiodan faith, known for hostility toward nonhumans and magic.
The cult of the Eternal Fire began as a local religion limited to Novigrad and its surrounding area.
About a century before the present, the Eternal Fire was a stern but relatively tolerant faith.
Eternal Fire priests taught that the sacred flame symbolized progress, light dispelling darkness, and hope for the future.
Early Eternal Fire doctrine tolerated other faiths except for blasphemy against the Eternal Fire or attempts to undermine its authority.
Those declared blasphemers or sorcerers who harmed others were burned at the stake by a special temple guard under early Eternal Fire rule.
As the Eternal Fire's influence grew, its hierarch, elected by a college, became the de facto ruler of Novigrad.
The Eternal Fire's temple guard evolved into an unchecked state security force with no secular oversight.
Under the Eternal Fire's growing power, false accusations, show trials, executions, and property confiscation became common.
Fear of black magic under the Eternal Fire evolved into hatred of all sorcery, nonhumans, and sorcerers, culminating in witch hunts that killed hundreds of innocents.
The Order of the Flaming Rose eventually became an extremist group devoted to racial persecution and witch hunts, turning against the humans and nonhumans it once swore to protect.
An Eternal Fire priest's sermon condemned women as sinful and demanded they be beaten, dressed modestly, and denied finery to curb supposed promiscuity.
New religious movements on the Continent increasingly claim exclusive possession of truth, branding other faiths as sinful apostasy.
Many new religious movements focus more on enforcing intolerant commandments than on offering spiritual support to their followers.
In remote regions, older faiths persist, such as the cult of the Ladies of the Wood in Velen, whose shrines are scattered through forests and villages there.
Necrophages include ghouls, foglets, rotfiends, and drowners, among other corpse-eating creatures.
Despite their name, most necrophages actively hunt live prey, including humans, rather than only eating carrion.
Some necrophage species bury or store their victims, letting them decay for days or weeks before eating them.
A common but false belief holds that necrophages are humans degenerated by generations of cannibalism.
Necrophages are actually post-Conjunction beings that arrived in the world due to the Conjunction of the Spheres.
Because necrophages have no natural ecological niche, killing them does not disrupt the balance of nature, so druids do not object to witchers exterminating them.
Wounds from necrophages carry high risk of tetanus infection and cadaverine contamination.
Necrophages that feed on plague victims can become disease carriers even though they are themselves immune to regular illnesses.
Many necrophages share traits like hairlessness, thin veiny skin, and atrophied sexual organs, suggesting a common post-Conjunction origin.
Ghouls form the main body of necrophages and include larger dangerous breeds like alghouls, graveirs, and cemetaurs.
Ghouls have a stooped posture, hypertrophied forelimbs, clawed hands adapted for digging, and strong jaws for cracking bones to eat marrow.
Rotfiends and greater rotfiends were once thought to be deformed ghouls but were later classified as a separate necrophage species.
Rotfiends stand upright with human-like limb proportions but have underdeveloped jaws and prefer eating corpses several months old.
Rotfiends rely mainly on smell to find victims since their heads are bloated and nearly eyeless.
Drowners live in both natural and artificial bodies of water, from rivers and lakes to sewers.
Popular belief holds that drowners are the risen corpses of drowned men, but they are actually post-Conjunction creatures.
Drowners and the drowned dead are strong swimmers who sense water vibrations and see well in low light.
Drowners prefer ambush attacks, dragging victims underwater and strangling them with clawed hands.
A folk tale describes a starving hamlet resorting to cannibalism during a harsh winter, eventually giving rise to a tribe that haunts graveyards and battlefields seeking human flesh.
Water hags live in wetlands, swamps, and bogs, building hovels of wood, mud, and reed or lairing in dug-out hollows.
Water hags have withered, slime-covered bodies, seaweed-like hair, crooked teeth, and werewolf-sized claws, and they throw balls of mud in combat.
According to folklore, water hags are naiads who fell in love with mortal men, lost their eternal youth, and slowly aged into hags.
Grave hags resemble tall, wizened old women with oversized heads, bulging eyes, and long clawed arms.
Grave hags dig up graves for skulls and bones to decorate their lairs or wear as amulets, leading to the mistaken belief they are female ghouls.
Unlike typical necrophages, grave hags actively hunt or lure victims, skin them, then cook and eat them like human dishes.
Vampires are not undead but beings that arrived in the world during the Conjunction of the Spheres.
Contrary to myth, sunlight is not lethal to most vampires, their bite does not create new vampires, and they are not repelled by garlic or holy water.
Vampires are traditionally split into higher vampires and lesser vampires, a widely used but technically imprecise classification.
Species like alps, mulas, katakans, bruxae, and nekurats are often grouped as higher vampires despite not being true higher vampires.
These lesser 'higher vampires' are resistant to sunlight, can disguise themselves as humans, and some can transform or use telepathy.
True higher vampires are an extremely powerful separate breed who nearly perfectly mimic humans, lacking shadows and mirror reflections as their only tell.
One higher vampire encountered did not trigger a reaction from a witcher medallion.
True higher vampires can turn into giant bats, become invisible, and mesmerize or put victims to sleep with their gaze.
True higher vampires are immune to sunlight, fire, and silver, and can regenerate even from beheading, dismemberment, or incineration, though it may take decades.
The term 'lesser vampires' commonly refers to fleders, ekimmaras, and garkains.
Fleders and ekimmaras are not native to the Northern Kingdoms but have expanded their range north across the Yaruga over the past couple decades.
Lesser vampires are more primitive and instinct-driven than higher vampires, vulnerable to sunlight, and hunt only at night.
Fleders will drink blood from and eat the flesh of sick victims and scavenge fresh corpses, behavior other vampire species avoid.
Fleders hibernate in crypts and abandoned buildings during winter, emerging to hunt on the first warm spring nights.
Vesemir reportedly said holy symbols are useless against vampires, at most insulting their religious feelings if they have any.
A wooden stake through the heart can harm a vampire due to their resilience, but a silver sword is the preferred weapon for witchers.
Most ghost stories arise from misidentified natural sounds, but genuine spiritual manifestations do occur as traumatic echoes of violent deaths.
Wraiths are vengeful ghosts of people who died violently or suddenly due to injustice, betrayal, or murder.
Murderers, oath breakers, and kinslayers can also become wraiths after death, not only their victims.
Ghosts of madmen or cruel people often become violent wraiths immediately, while others take time to transform.
Wraiths formed from murder victims may initially seek help from the living for revenge or restitution before fading away, unless powerful emotions bind them to the world.
One theory holds that a wraith's grotesque form reflects growing madness distorting both its inner and outer self over decades or centuries.
Folk belief holds that noonwraiths and nightwraiths are the ghosts of women who died violently before or after their weddings.

A wraith ritual to prevent a restless dead from rising involves drinking moonshine, wrapping a thornapple rod around the corpse's neck, driving nails through its heart, and filling its mouth with poppy seeds before reburial.
Noonwraiths appear on bright, warm days as tanned girls or hags in white robes, sometimes wearing wedding wreaths, preying on field workers and children.
Nightwraiths are active at night, especially during a full moon, ambushing late travelers or sneaking into homes to attack sleepers.
Both noonwraiths and nightwraiths drain life from victims while swirling around them in a mockery of a wedding dance.
Hybrids are monsters combining traits of two or more creatures, with debated origins either from the Conjunction of the Spheres or predating it.
Griffins resemble a cross between a large cat and a predatory bird, nesting on inaccessible mountain peaks and preying on large hoofed mammals.
Griffins are highly territorial and will attack travelers, merchant caravans, and shepherds who encroach on their territory.
The archgriffin is a rare, extremely aggressive griffin subspecies capable of spitting acid balls that cause severe burns.
Harpies have the bodies of old women combined with bird wings, talons, and beaks, and they build colonies on inaccessible cliffs.
Harpies are omnivorous, generally attack smaller prey by diving from above, but can gang up on larger prey including armed humans.
The cockatrice, also called the scoffin, is a rare ornithosaur combining traits of birds and reptiles, supposedly hatched from an egg laid by a rooster and incubated by snakes.
Contrary to superstition, a cockatrice's gaze cannot kill or petrify; its real threats are its beak and sharp tail used in ambush or combat.
Curses require a human caster with sufficiently concentrated will and strong emotion, similar in mechanism to prayer, though the final effect is delayed and rarely matches the literal words spoken.
Creatures called 'the Damned' result from curses, including strigas and botchlings, as well as humans cursed through contact with an original victim, such as werewolves.
Witchers are sometimes hired to lift curses on such creatures rather than simply kill them, depending on the circumstances.
Werewolves are terianthropes, humans able to transform into wolf or half-wolf hybrid form, usually during a full moon.
Some lycanthropes retain control and avoid people while transformed, while most either embrace bloodlust or black out during transformation.
A competing theory suggests lycanthropy may be hereditary rather than purely a curse, since some werewolves are born with the trait and can fully control transformation.
Werewolves born with hereditary lycanthropy are nearly impossible to cure unless they cooperate willingly.
Botchlings are created when an unwanted child dies and is not properly buried; they are about one and a half feet tall.
A botchling hides under beds and drains vitality from pregnant women, causing fever and weakness before attacking directly and killing mother and unborn child.
When threatened, a botchling can transform into a deformed crawling humanoid to attack with bites and claws.
Giving a botchling a proper burial lifts its curse and turns it into a protective household spirit called a lubberkin.
A striga is created from a curse placed on a pregnant woman, causing her child to become a monster instead of surviving as human.
A striga rises from its grave years after death to prowl near its burial ground, and despite being small and hunched, it is supernaturally fast and strong.
Strigas prefer eating internal organs, especially liver and heart, and are more aggressive during the full moon.
Lifting a striga's curse requires waiting at its burial site through the night until the third rooster crow at dawn catches it outside its coffin, returning it to human form.
Draconids are a numerous monster order including at least half a dozen true dragon species plus lesser draconids, long native to the Continent's ecosystem.
